title: CRA Ten-Year Update Vault for Vendors
one_liner: An escrow-plus-hosting service that keeps a small vendor's signed security updates, vulnerability intake and orphaned open-source dependencies alive for the EU Cyber Resilience Act's ten-year obligation if the vendor folds or an upstream dies.
customer: Small EU-selling firmware, IoT and software vendors (1-50 staff) with no security team, and the enterprise buyers and OEMs who will demand proof of continuity before they buy from them.
problem: CRA reporting duties started 2026-09-11 and the main obligations bite 2027-12-11, with no size exemption. A solo German software founder on HN (Sept 1, 2026) calls the requirement that security updates stay available for ten years, or the support period if longer, a critical burden, and notes reporting duties continue after support ends. Harmonised standards aren't published yet (core standards due Oct 31, 2026). Open-source upstreams also vanish: MinIO (61.3k stars) was archived on 2026-04-25 with no binaries, and 'no fork has gained traction'.
solution: Three parts. (1) Escrow: a reproducible-build environment, SBOM/VEX and split-custody signing keys held by the vault, released on contractual trigger events (insolvency, abandonment, twelve months without a patch). (2) Continuity hosting: a signed-update endpoint and advisory feed that stays online for ten years, plus a vulnerability-report intake and drafts for the EU single reporting platform. (3) Dependency lifeboat: patch backports and maintained forks of orphaned components that customers depend on (MinIO first). Vendors get a 'continuity certificate' to attach to tenders.
why_now: Reporting obligations are 17 days old as of today, standards are still being written, and small vendors are asking on HN what to do. The EU's own guidance creates open-source 'stewards' who face obligations but are exempt from fines, while manufacturers carry the burden, so the market will look for a commercial steward.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and hosting fee per product (EUR 1.5k-6k), a per-release fee, trigger-event activation fee, and dependency-lifeboat support contracts priced per node.
non_obvious_insight: The CRA turns 'what if you disappear?' from a founder worry into a legal duty, and escrow-style insurance sells to both the vendor and the buyer who fears the vendor's death; the compliance-tooling crowd (scanners, SBOM dashboards) does not cover it. Evidence: Ask HN by a one-person vendor on the ten-year update rule, harmonised standards timing and no size exemption (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49520688). The EU says stewards are not subject to administrative fines (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-open-source), with the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates at https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act. Linux Foundation research finds most open-source respondents unfamiliar with the CRA and its deadlines (https://linuxfoundation.org/research/cra-readiness). Greg Kroah-Hartman's explainer says the burden lands on commercial manufacturers (https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/30/cyber_reiliance_act_opinion_column/). Upstream death example: https://github.com/minio/minio.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the escrow and trigger-event contract template with an EU tech lawyer, and prototype a reproducible-build capture for one embedded Linux and one Go or Rust project. Days 10-30: post a plain-English 'CRA ten-year problem' guide on HN, the Open Regulatory Compliance working group hub and embedded-vendor communities, and offer 10 founders a free continuity assessment. Sell 3 paid pilot vaults at a founder price of EUR 1k a year. In parallel, publish a MinIO advisory-and-patch feed to test paying demand for the lifeboat.

title: Time-to-First-Part: Install Readiness for Machine Dealers
one_liner: A pre-delivery site-scan and commissioning package that gets backlogged machines cutting parts weeks sooner.
customer: Machine-tool, laser and robot dealers and OEM sales teams, plus 20-200 employee manufacturers buying their first big machine.
problem: Unfilled capital-goods orders sit at $953B after a record $85.9B in July orders. Much of it lands in old buildings with no as-built drawings. Machines arrive to floors, doors, crane paths and utility drops that cannot take them, so crated $500k machines sit idle. Dealers often get paid only at acceptance.
solution: A 20-minute phone or LiDAR walkthrough becomes an as-built model. Software checks the machine footprint, door and aisle clearance and rigging path, flags slab and vibration issues (with a ground-penetrating-radar partner), lists air, coolant and chip-handling needs, and produces a rigging plan and punch list. It can also dispatch vetted riggers and millwrights.
why_now: Reshoring is happening inside existing walls, the equipment backlog is at a record, and riggers and millwrights are scarce. Phone-based 3D capture (LiDAR, Gaussian splats) has matured.
revenue_model: $1.2-3k per site package, paid by the dealer or bundled into the machine price. 10-15% referral on rigging. Dealer team subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dealers get paid at acceptance, so time-to-first-part is their cash-flow metric and they will pay to shorten it. The unfilled-order backlog hides a second backlog of installed-but-not-producing machines.
first_30_days: Sign three regional dealers (CNC, laser or robot) for a pilot. Do 10 scans with iPhones. Produce a sample report. Measure install days saved against comparable installs.

title: Two A.M. Any-Tradition Rites and Interpreter Line
one_liner: A 24/7 dispatch of vetted ritual specialists and death-trained interpreters for families outside the majority faith, sold to hospices and palliative units.
customer: Hospices, hospital palliative units and nursing homes in metros with large immigrant and non-Christian populations. They pay a monthly retainer plus per-dispatch fees.
problem: Most hospice chaplains are generalists trained in a Christian or interfaith pastoral model, and chaplain FTEs are among the first things cut when margins tighten. When an imam, Hindu priest, Buddhist monk, Sikh granthi, Hmong ritual specialist, Orthodox priest, or Native elder is needed, the family often gets the default chaplain, and the ritual windows are short and unforgiving. Some rites happen only before death, others require that the body not be moved or touched for hours, or that someone be present continuously. Standard hospice protocol says 'call the funeral home now.' Language is the second failure. Family members interpret for the patient and quietly soften bad news. In many languages the word 'dying' is unsayable. Interpreter contracts are priced per minute and built for clinic visits, with no death vocabulary or truth-telling norm training.
solution: A dispatch line and app for the hospice chaplain or on-call nurse. It connects to a vetted, paid roster of ritual specialists by tradition and language who can arrive or join by video, plus a small pool of interpreters who have completed a 40-hour end-of-life interpreting course (death vocabulary, family-filtering, cultural norms about naming prognosis). A one-page 'rite card' library is loaded into the hospice's EHR or intranet for each tradition. It gives the practical do's and don'ts: how to position the patient, what not to do to the body, who should not touch it, how long to wait before calling the funeral home, and what the family may ask for. Start with one metro and 4 to 6 traditions.
why_now: AI translation is tempting hospices to cut interpreter budgets, while civil-rights language-access rules (Section 1557 of the ACA as revised in 2024) push toward qualified interpreters and human review of machine translation for critical content. Confirm the current status of those rules. The older-adult population is more foreign-born and religiously diverse than a decade ago, and the unaffiliated 'nones' need secular rituals too. Chaplain staffing is shrinking. Consolidated hospice chains want scalable ways to meet 'emotional and spiritual support' quality measures.
revenue_model: A monthly retainer of $1,500 to $4,000 per hospice or hospital for 24/7 access. Per-dispatch fees ($150 to $300 to the specialist, with a 30 to 40 percent platform margin). Premium per-minute interpreting rates above standard telephone rates. Training and certification revenue from the interpreter course, sold to language-service companies and hospitals. Family fees are not charged.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not spiritual care in general but time-critical, tradition-specific competence at the exact hour of death, which a generalist chaplain honestly cannot supply. Family interpreters are the largest hidden source of bad-news distortion in end-of-life care. Whoever builds the roster and the interpreter standard owns a moat that AI translation cannot cross, because the value is trust and ritual authority, not words.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where you know the communities (for example Minneapolis–St. Paul for Hmong, Somali and Karen families, or Houston or Queens for a wider mix). Recruit 20 to 25 ritual specialists and interpreters through mosque, temple and community boards, and pay them a small stipend for a 3-hour training on hospice basics. Build the rite-card library with their input. Sign two hospices to a free 60-day pilot on a shared phone number, then convert them to a retainer and use their case counts in a pitch to the next five.

title: SOX Evidence Packs for Agent-Run Controls
one_liner: Control libraries, walkthrough scripts and test evidence that let auditors accept AI agents inside financial close, AP and reconciliations.
customer: Controllers, SOX program managers and internal audit at US public companies ($500M-$10B revenue) piloting agents in finance, plus mid-tier audit firms that must test them.
problem: As of mid-2026 the PCAOB has no AI-specific standard. Auditors ask how agent actions are authorized, logged and reviewed, and whether agent-generated walkthroughs count as sufficient evidence. FEI's Committee on Corporate Reporting published an AI-in-ICFR framework in June 2026, but finance teams have no packaged controls or evidence format.
solution: A library of agent-specific controls mapped to COSO 2013 (access, prompt and model change management, completeness, override monitoring), with test scripts, sampling templates and an evidence collector that exports action logs, approval trails and change tickets in auditor-ready format. Start with a pre-interim readiness assessment.
why_now: Calendar-2026 audits are entering interim testing, the June 2026 FEI framework gives a hook, and a standards vacuum means the first accepted evidence format wins.
revenue_model: $20-$60k readiness assessments, $3-$8k/month evidence subscriptions, and license deals with audit firms.
non_obvious_insight: In a standards vacuum, the first packaged evidence format an audit firm accepts becomes the de facto standard, as SOC 2 report formats did for cloud. Auditors are also under pressure to have an answer.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 former Big-4 SOX auditors and write 25 agent controls. Run free readiness workshops for 10 controllers already piloting agents in AP or close, and convert 2-3 to paid assessments.

title: Condition-Based Kitchen Exhaust Cleaning Sensors
one_liner: Duct-mounted grease-film sensor pods, sold through hood-cleaning contractors, that predict when a restaurant's exhaust system actually needs cleaning and prove the cleaning was done.
customer: Independent commercial kitchen exhaust cleaning contractors (5-50 technicians) as the channel and first payer. End users are restaurants, hotels, hospital and campus kitchens, and ghost-kitchen operators, with commercial property insurers as a downstream discount payer.
problem: NFPA 96 sets calendar cleaning intervals from monthly to annual by cooking type, but real grease buildup varies enormously by menu (wok, charbroil and fryer kitchens versus sandwich shops). The result is over-cleaning in some places and dangerous under-cleaning in others. Restaurants can't see inside their ducts, so they can't verify that hard-to-reach plenum and duct runs were really cleaned. Grease is a leading cause of restaurant fires and property insurers increasingly want documentation.
solution: A retrofit pod at the hood plenum and an access panel, with temperature, airflow or differential-pressure, fan-current and a capacitive grease-film sensor. It uses BLE or LoRa to a small gateway. An edge model outputs 'days to cleaning threshold' and schedules the contractor. After each cleaning the pod records a post-clean baseline, which becomes tamper-evident proof for the restaurant, the fire inspector and the insurer. Start with sensors outside the duct interior (plenum, access panel) to avoid grease and heat survivability problems.
why_now: Cheap MEMS and capacitive sensing plus LoRa/BLE make a sub-USD-100 pod feasible. Documentation expectations in recent NFPA 96 editions and commercial property insurance hardening push restaurants toward provable maintenance. Contractors face thin margins and want stickier recurring contracts.
revenue_model: Hardware at USD 180-350 per hood, or leased. Subscription of USD 25-45 per month per hood, with a 30% revenue share to the contractor who resells and installs. Pilot insurer premium-credit program. Contractor-side scheduling and route-optimization software as an upsell.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the cleaner, not the restaurant. Monitoring turns a commodity route-calendar service into a data-backed recurring contract and cuts wasted truck rolls. The most valuable reading is not the continuous alert but the after-clean baseline, because the actual pain is 'did they really clean the duct?' That is a trust problem no one solves today.
first_30_days: Prototype a pod from off-the-shelf sensors. Recruit three cleaning contractors through the International Kitchen Exhaust Cleaning Association network and offer free pods on 10 hoods each. Log grease-accumulation curves by cuisine type for 60-90 days. Show the contractors their own before/after evidence, then sell the first paid subscriptions with revenue share.

title: Battery-Islanded Feeders Instead of Undergrounding
one_liner: Sell utilities islandable rural feeders powered by enrolled home batteries as a cheaper alternative to undergrounding and repeated wildfire power shutoffs.
customer: Wildfire-exposed utilities and co-ops (California, Pacific Northwest, Colorado, Hawaii), funded from wildfire-mitigation capex. Tribal and community microgrids are a secondary buyer.
problem: Undergrounding costs roughly $2-3M or more per mile, and public safety power shutoffs cut power to thousands of homes for days. Home batteries are common (46% storage attach), but each only serves its own house, and utilities cannot use them to keep a whole feeder alive.
solution: A feeder-level controller, smart switch and grid-forming coordination software that lets a segment island when upstream is de-energized, with enrolled home batteries powering critical loads. The same software runs normal VPP dispatch to pay for itself. The utility contracts it as a non-wires wildfire alternative.
why_now: 140k batteries delivered 580 MW on Sept 9, grid-forming inverters are now standard, wildfire budgets are large, and affordability limits undergrounding.
revenue_model: $150-400 per customer-year availability payment from the utility, a controller lease, and VPP revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The battery is already in the house, and the missing pieces are coordination and a switch. Utilities cannot earn a return on efficiency, but they can on wildfire mitigation capex, and you are competing against $3M per mile.
first_30_days: Approach small co-ops and munis in fire-prone areas. Pick a 200-home feeder with at least 30% battery attach. Propose a paid $40k feasibility study and a pilot using existing devices. Partner with a microgrid-controller vendor.

title: Group Apprenticeship Employer for Data-Center Electricians
one_liner: An Australian-style group training organization that employs apprentices and rents them to small electrical and plumbing contractors, absorbing the paperwork, wage risk and poaching risk.
customer: Small and mid-size electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors (5-50 staff) in data-center and construction-boom metros; apprentices, including underemployed college grads.
problem: Electricians have about 72.7k openings a year, boosted by data-center demand, but the 4-5 year path is bottlenecked by employer sponsors and pre-apprenticeship screening. Small contractors cannot carry multi-year risk, admin and classroom scheduling, and apprentices are poached after year one or two. Meanwhile 42% of recent grads are underemployed and have no route in.
solution: The group sponsor is the registered-apprenticeship sponsor and employer of record. It screens and recruits, pays wages and workers' comp, rotates apprentices across host contractors, schedules related instruction with a community college or JATC (up to 49% of instruction can be outsourced to employers or unions under the new apprenticeship rules), and bills hosts hourly. Market a career-changer track to laid-off grads.
why_now: AI data-center construction is pulling electricians while AI is closing entry-level white-collar doors, creating both demand and a motivated recruit pool. Workforce Pell gives apprenticeship-linked programs a fast lane, making college partners eager.
revenue_model: A 20-30% markup over apprentice wage cost billed to host contractors (about 15-20% gross margin, staffing-style), plus state apprenticeship incentives and college partnership fees.
non_obvious_insight: Contractors do not lack applicants; they lack appetite for multi-year risk and administration. Splitting the employer role from the host job site removes the constraint, as group training organizations did in Australia.
first_30_days: Choose one data-center metro. Sign 5 small contractors to LOIs for 10 apprentice seats. Partner with an existing IEC or ABC chapter for registration and compliance. Recruit 30 candidates from local underemployed grads and start an 8-week evening pre-apprenticeship course.

title: Hotel Strike Early-Warning for Event Planners
one_liner: A subscription database and parametric cover that tells meeting and group planners which contracted hotels' labour contracts expire before their event, and pays out if a strike hits.
customer: Association and corporate meeting planners, incentive houses, sports and event organisers and tour operators that contract 100+ room-night blocks 12-24 months ahead.
problem: Chicago hotel workers authorised a strike at 85%, potentially the largest in the city's history, and a Seattle Hilton strike lasted 85 days. Planners contract blocks years ahead and learn about labour risk from the news. Strike coverage under contract clauses is vague, and relocating an event on short notice costs heavily.
solution: Track union contract expirations, strike votes and bargaining status per property, from union pages, filings and news. Score each hotel and date for strike risk, alert planners, and provide a labour-disruption clause template. Later add parametric cover underwritten by an MGA that pays per room-night if a strike affects a contracted property.
why_now: Hotel labour unrest is elevated in 2026, hotel costs have repriced sharply, and hotel operators are cutting staff citing AI (Mews cut 15%). Planners are more exposed to relocation than ever.
revenue_model: USD 3-8K per year per planning team, cover premiums of about 1.5-3% of block value, and broker fees.
non_obvious_insight: A strike is a scheduled event, not a surprise. Contract expiry dates are public, yet the buyers of long-dated blocks bear the tail risk and nobody prices it.
first_30_days: Compile a spreadsheet of union contract expirations for the top 40 US convention cities from union local sites and news. Publish a free '2027 events at risk' report to planner communities, then convert responders to a USD 2K annual subscription. Line up an MGA for the cover after the first 10 customers.

title: The 4 A.M. Ride Guild
one_liner: A dispatch network of night-owl local drivers, paid per ride by hospitals and jails, that gets rural patients and released inmates home at hours when Uber and Medicaid rides do not exist.
customer: Critical access hospitals and their foundations, county jails, domestic violence shelters, crisis stabilization units, and Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans (through value-added benefits). Paid per ride, then by plan contract.
problem: A patient is discharged from a rural ER at 4am. She came by ambulance, her car is 30 miles away, and no taxi, Uber or Lyft exists. Medicaid non-emergency transport needs 24-48 hours notice and does not cover ER discharge. So she sits in the waiting room, a nurse drives her home (against policy), a relative is woken up, or the hospital admits her to observation for 'social reasons', which costs thousands. Jails release people at midnight with no ride, and domestic violence shelters have the same problem in reverse.
solution: A dispatch line (an SMS and phone flow with a human on call, then an app) that promises a driver within 30 minutes anywhere in a county between 10pm and 8am. Supply comes from people who are awake anyway: workers finishing third shift at plants, retired EMTs, volunteer firefighters and off-duty deputies. Riders can be dropped at a hospital, home or shelter, with documented handoff for CMS discharge planning. Add wheelchair-capable vehicles later. Insurance is hired and non-owned auto coverage, and drivers are background checked.
why_now: Rural hospitals are under pressure from Medicaid cuts and closing service lines, so avoiding costly observation stays and unsafe discharges matters more. Rural Health Transformation Program funds can pay for transport and access. Uber Health, Lyft and NEMT brokers are still thin at rural night hours, and the gap is a supply problem software alone cannot fix. Gig-style dispatch and background-check tooling is now cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: The hospital pays $85-110 per ride and the driver gets $55-65. A monthly minimum of $500-1,500 per facility guarantees driver availability, similar to a retainer. Later add Medicaid MCO and Medicare Advantage value-added benefit contracts. The ride log also supports the hospital's safe-discharge documentation.
non_obvious_insight: Nurses know that the ride is what actually gates a safe discharge at night, and that the hospital quietly pays for it in nurse gas money, observation admissions and ambulance runs. Transport startups assume demand is the hard part. In rural night hours supply is the hard part, and the winning move is recruiting people who are awake at 4am and paying them a guaranteed minimum. Hospital foundations, whose donors like 'getting Grandma home safe', are also a surprisingly easy first funder.
first_30_days: Sign one hospital and one sheriff's office for a pilot with a prepaid $1,000 retainer each. Recruit 15 drivers through third-shift plants, fire department Facebook groups and truck stops. Run dispatch manually via a Twilio group text with the founder on call. Get a hired-and-non-owned auto policy through a commercial broker and run background checks through a screening vendor. Track time to ride and observation stays avoided, and use those to pitch a second and third hospital.

title: After-School Shop Clubs Run by Retired Tradespeople
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing/skilled-trades/home services x Parenting/childcare deserts/Gen Alpha/kids and AI-screens
one_liner: Screen-free after-school care for ages 10-15 inside idle trade-school and union shops, staffed by retired journeymen who teach kids to build real things.
customer: Parents of 10-15-year-olds paying about $180-260 a month, plus sponsors (contractor associations, distributors, JATCs and local subs) paying $150-300 per enrolled kid as a recruiting pipeline. State child-care subsidy vouchers where the program is licensed.
problem: School-age care from 3 to 6pm is scarce, and Gen Alpha teens fill it with phones and AI companions (72% of US teens have used them) while under-16 social bans leak. Most of the trades labor gap is retirements, and the pipeline is thinner than headlines suggest (the enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage). Community-college and JATC shops sit empty after 3pm. Retired tradespeople lose purpose and have no channel to pass on skills.
solution: Run a licensed or license-exempt (per state rule) after-school program in partner shops. One certified childcare lead plus paid retired journeyman mentors ($25-30/hr from sponsor funds) run projects such as tiny houses, cabinetry, wiring boards and plumbing trees. Phones stay in lockers. Older kids earn micro-credentials (OSHA-10 at 16, NCCER Core) and sponsors get first look. A small local team can run in three shops in year one.
why_now: Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia have under-16 bans, US school phone bans cover 12 states, and parents want credible offline options. ROAD to Housing Act standard plans and manufactured-home reforms are creating build content and demand for skilled set crews. The retirement wave is driving most of the ABC 349K and 456K worker gap.
revenue_model: Tuition $180-260 per child per month, sponsor fees $150-300 per child per month (or lump-sum program sponsorship), subsidy vouchers where eligible, and mentor stipends funded through sponsorship.
non_obvious_insight: The apprenticeship pipeline's real bottleneck is exposure and mentors before age 16, not training seats. Idle shops, retired mentors and parents desperate for screen-free care are three underused assets that pay for each other. A contractor who pays $3K to keep a local kid in the trades over two years is spending less than the cost of one bad hire.
first_30_days: Partner with one community college, ABC or IEC chapter training center. Recruit three retired journeymen and confirm the state licensing exemption (or license a school-age program). Run an 8-week pilot three afternoons a week for 12 kids at $180 a month, with $500 sponsorships from five local subs, and fill the waitlist through local parent Facebook groups.

title: Flooded Homeowners Meet Wetland Mitigation Buyers
one_liner: Match repeatedly flooded homeowners who want out with wetland and stream mitigation bankers who need floodplain land and can pay faster than federal buyouts.
customer: Compensatory-mitigation bankers, in-lieu-fee programs and land trusts (acquisition fee), counties and cities with repetitive-loss properties (program-management contracts), and homeowners (free, receive offers).
problem: Federal buyouts take years, and funding has become unreliable since the 2025 cancellation of BRIC and subsequent court fights. Meanwhile flood insurance premiums keep rising under Risk Rating 2.0 and repeat-flood homes are hard to sell. Mitigation bankers must buy contiguous floodplain and riparian land to earn Clean Water Act credits but usually source rural farmland by landman. They do not see suburban stream corridors lined with flooded homes as inventory.
solution: Screen NFIP repetitive-loss data, lidar and flood models and the RIBITS bank and credit ledger to find stream reaches where clusters of repeat-flood parcels adjoin high-credit-price watersheds. Run homeowner outreach and assemble willing sellers into a single package for a banker or land trust. The homes are demolished and the floodplain restored, with credits sold to permit-seeking developers and transport agencies.
why_now: Federal buyout money is slow and unpredictable, insurance repricing keeps rising, and data-center, industrial and transport permitting is driving demand for Section 404 mitigation credits. Public flood, lidar and ledger data make cluster screening possible for a small team.
revenue_model: Success fee of 2% to 3% of purchase price or $10k to $25k per assembled cluster (via a licensed real-estate partner), $2k to $5k a month screening subscription for bankers, and $50k to $150k municipal program-management contracts.
non_obvious_insight: A chain of flooded houses is exactly the restoration real estate a mitigation banker cannot otherwise get, and the funder of last resort can be a regulated compliance market rather than the taxpayer. This is a Clean Water Act compliance market, not a voluntary carbon-style offset.
first_30_days: Map 50 candidate reaches from public repetitive-loss, lidar and RIBITS data. Call 10 bankers and land trusts with a shopping list. Mail 200 homeowners on one reach. Sign a pilot with one banker and one county for program management.

title: Camera-Free Nap-Room Proof-of-Supervision
one_liner: Start with NFC crib tags that create tamper-evident safe-sleep check logs for childcare centers, then add 60GHz radar that verifies presence and breathing without any camera.
customer: Childcare centers' infant and toddler rooms, small chains, childcare liability insurers and brokers, and licensing agencies.
problem: Safe-sleep checks are handwritten logs that can be filled in after the fact. Sleep supervision failures drive licensing violations, insurance claims and tragedies. Cameras raise privacy objections. After abuse incidents at premium chains (Bright Horizons NYC, per the brief), parents and insurers want proof that supervision happened, not just cameras.
solution: Phase 1: teachers tap a badge on an NFC tag at each crib every interval, producing a timestamped, tamper-evident log and alerts for missed checks. Phase 2: a ceiling-mounted mmWave radar puck detects presence, motion and position class with no images, cross-checking the log. Positioned as compliance logging, not a medical device.
why_now: Low-cost 60GHz radar chips and infant-sensing research are now mature. Insurers are tightening abuse and molestation coverage (from memory). Public attention to childcare safety is high after the 2025-26 incidents.
revenue_model: $20-45 per crib per month plus a $150 radar device, with insurer premium-credit revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The value is proof of supervision, not detection. Detection claims invite FDA regulation and false-assurance liability, while insurers and inspectors will pay for un-fakeable evidence that checks happened.
first_30_days: Build the NFC tag and phone app. Pilot in 3 infant rooms. Talk to 2 childcare insurers or brokers about premium credits. Prototype breathing detection on an evaluation radar board with adult volunteers and a manikin, never infants.

title: Belonging Pods to Cut Home-Care Aide Turnover
one_liner: Weekly peer pods and buddy mentors for isolated home-care aides, sold to agencies as a turnover-reduction service priced per retained aide.
customer: Home-care agencies (tens of thousands in the US, 50-500 aides each) and the Medicaid managed-care and Medicare Advantage plans that fund them, paying $8-15 per aide per month.
problem: Aides work alone in strangers' homes, with annual turnover often 65-80% and a replacement cost of several thousand dollars each. Engagement surveys measure isolation but fix nothing. Clients die and aides grieve without support. The workforce hired to cure elder loneliness is itself lonely, and agencies experience the pain only as attrition.
solution: Pods of 6 aides grouped by geography and shift, with a weekly 30-minute voice huddle (dial-in works, no app needed), a paid peer mentor per 30 aides, a monthly in-person meal, a 'hard visit' debrief line, and scripts for client death. A dashboard shows pod attendance against 90-day retention for the agency.
why_now: The aide shortage is acute. Immigration enforcement in 2025-26 is reported to be thinning a workforce in which roughly a quarter are immigrants. Plans and agencies want cheap retention levers, and loneliness is now legitimized as a health metric.
revenue_model: Per-aide monthly subscription with a performance kicker tied to retention, plus facilitator staffing margin. Later contracts with managed-care plans.
non_obvious_insight: Agencies do not buy belonging, they buy retention. Framing belonging as a turnover product with a hard ROI (each retained aide saves thousands) unlocks a budget that wellness and loneliness framing never will.
first_30_days: Sign three agencies with 100+ aides through state home-care association chapters. Run pods for about 60 aides and compare 90-day retention against a control group. Charge $6 per aide per month for the pilot.

title: Dog Walkers as Repeat-Pass Sidewalk Inspectors
one_liner: Pay dog walkers a few dollars a day to mount a phone on their chest and sell the resulting block-by-block sidewalk condition layer to cities, utilities, and delivery-robot operators.
customer: City public works and ADA coordinators (mid-size cities of 100k to 500k people first), plus fiber and utility contractors and sidewalk delivery-robot operators as second buyers. Walkers are the paid supply side.
problem: Cities are legally on the hook to inventory sidewalks and curb ramps and fix trip hazards. Today that means an expensive contractor van or LiDAR survey every 5 to 10 years, or 311 complaints that skew toward loud, wealthy neighborhoods. Residential side streets go stale, and nobody sees a slab heave, a missing curb ramp, or a new obstruction until someone sues or gets hurt.
solution: A harness or chest mount plus a background app that runs during walks. It records geotagged video, and an on-device model flags heaved slabs, missing or noncompliant curb ramps, obstructions, standing water, and broken glass. Faces and plates are blurred on the phone and nothing is recorded near windows or interiors. Walkers earn per validated mile (roughly $1 a mile, so about $8 to $15 a day for something they already do). The city gets a rolling map with change detection, exported to its existing GIS or asset-management tools. A free 'dog hazard' layer (glass, bait or poison reports, hot pavement, off-leash aggressive dogs) gives walkers and owners a reason to adopt it. I have not verified current competitors or municipal pricing, so both should be checked before the pitch.
why_now: In 2026 a phone can run a decent defect-detection model offline, which was not practical a few years ago. Cities face ongoing ADA sidewalk obligations and litigation risk with tight budgets, which favors cheap continuous data over big one-off surveys. Driver-sourced street imagery (Hivemapper and Nexar style) has proven that crowds get paid for mapping, but the pedestrian tier is essentially unclaimed.
revenue_model: Annual municipal data subscription, or per-mile survey pricing that undercuts contractor quotes, at roughly $20k to $150k a year per city. Secondary sales of the same data to utilities, telecom build QA, and robot-delivery mapping. Walkers are paid about 30 to 40 percent of revenue as per-mile payouts.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody walks a residential sidewalk more than a dog walker: the same 3 to 5 miles, five days a week, at a slow pace, with eyes on the ground because dogs eat everything. The scarce asset in infrastructure data is not coverage, it is repeat passes, which is what makes change detection possible. That is exactly what a walker's fixed route produces for free.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 to 20 walkers through local pet-sitter Facebook groups and Nextdoor, since they are already clustered by neighborhood. Build the capture app with a cheap phone mount and an open sidewalk-defect model fine-tuned on public sidewalk datasets. Map about 200 miles of one neighborhood, then take a before-and-after sample to a city ADA or transportation coordinator. Offer a free neighborhood pilot with a cost comparison against contractor rates, and aim for a small pilot purchase order under the city's simple-purchase threshold.

title: Standby Mass-Fatality Cooler Network for Counties
one_liner: A retainer-based network of vetted funeral homes with cooler space, vans and chain-of-custody training that counties and hospital coalitions can activate when the morgue overflows.
customer: County emergency managers, medical examiner and coroner offices, regional Health Care Coalitions and hospital systems. They fund it through preparedness grants, state emergency-management budgets and hospital readiness budgets.
problem: Mass-fatality plans routinely say 'coordinate with local funeral directors', which is a handshake with no contract, no capacity inventory, no shared identification protocol and no payment. ME planning guides size storage at roughly 1.5x average daily caseload plus a 25% surge buffer, so a heat wave, hurricane, flood or outbreak blows through it. Counties then scramble for refrigerated trailers, which are undignified, poorly tracked, and a magnet for misidentification scandals. Funeral homes are willing to help but can't say what they can commit and dread not being paid.
solution: Enroll 10-30 funeral homes per region. Run a capacity survey (cooler slots, bariatric capability, generators, on-call staff, vehicles). Train them in ID and chain-of-custody basics, personal-effects logging and family-notification etiquette, a DMORT-lite curriculum. Credential their licenses and insurance. Provide a shared dashboard and case-tracking app with unique IDs, tags, photos and effects logs that exports to the ME's systems. Sell the county or coalition a one-to-three-year readiness retainer with an annual tabletop exercise and pre-negotiated per-diem activation rates. Add an 'everyday overflow' service for ME backlogs, such as holiday weekends and opioid or heat spikes, at per-case rates, which turns readiness into recurring revenue.
why_now: Federal disaster support is being pushed toward states and counties, so local preparedness is becoming a locally funded line item. Record heat deaths in the Southwest and busy hurricane seasons keep overloading morgues. ME offices are visibly overflowing, and new facilities such as Jacksonville's in 2026 are being built with triple capacity. Forensic pathologist shortages slow releases and keep bodies in coolers longer.
revenue_model: Annual readiness retainer of $15,000-$60,000 per county or coalition region, with a stipend of about $3,000-$8,000 flowing to each participating funeral home. Activation per diem of $75-$150 per body per day. Overflow per-case fees. $8,000-$15,000 for tabletop exercises and training. Software license for the tracking app.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset in a mass-fatality event isn't refrigerated trucks, it's trusted, licensed humans with cooled rooms already in every zip code, and they sit about 70% idle. No one has ever paid funeral homes to stay ready. Public trust collapses over identification and chain-of-custody errors, not storage, and funeral directors are the only civilians who do that work every day.
first_30_days: Pick one heat- and hurricane-exposed region. Recruit 10-15 funeral homes through the state funeral directors' association. Write a 12-page letter-of-commitment and capacity template. Book meetings with five county emergency managers and two Health Care Coalition coordinators (public directories). Offer a $7,500 paid tabletop exercise plus regional capacity map, priced under many small-purchase thresholds. Convert the exercise participants to a retainer proposal.

title: Data-Center Community Benefits That Fund Rural Vets
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & the grid x Pets & animal health
one_liner: An intermediary that packages animal-care compacts (vet loan repayment, mobile clinics, low-cost care days, shelter energy upgrades) as community-benefit commitments for data-center developers fighting local opposition.
customer: Data-center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams siting campuses in rural and exurban counties, plus county officials. Payment is a program management fee on the pledged benefit package.
problem: Seven in ten Americans oppose data centers in their community (Gallup) and New York has imposed a statewide hyperscale moratorium. Delays are extremely costly (a delayed 60 MW commissioning costs about $14M a month). Typical community benefits are abstract (tax revenue, school grants). Meanwhile rural counties face a vet shortage (91,100 US vets, only about 3,100 openings a year) and vet costs are the single most visible affordability pressure for pet and livestock owners.
solution: Design and run a neutral 'Vet Access Compact' per county: loan repayment or salary top-ups for rural vets and techs, a solar-battery mobile clinic, quarterly low-cost vaccine and spay/neuter days, and shelter energy upgrades. Administer it with measurable outcomes (appointments, wait times), match it with philanthropic dollars where possible, and give the developer credible, publishable reporting. Optionally link the developer's backup power to the clinic's resilience.
why_now: Data-center opposition and moratoria surged in 2026, and electricity affordability is a midterm issue. Duffield's $250M commitment and PetSmart Charities' pledge provide matching money. New vet-professional tiers (Colorado's VPA) expand who can be funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% program design and administration fee on $1-5M multi-year packages, grant-matching and outcome-reporting retainers, and implementation fees for mobile clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Animals are one of the few bipartisan, hyper-local issues that reach every county, and a $2M program is a rounding error against a $1B campus. It pairs capital-rich, trust-poor developers with trust-rich, capital-poor local vets who also speak at public hearings.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with pending data-center hearings on the public calendar. Call the county veterinary association and extension office to map the gaps. Produce a one-page compact and pitch it to developers' community-affairs leads. Sell a $15-30K design study as the first paid engagement. Avoid contingent fees tied to permit outcomes.

title: Drought-to-Curtailment Forecasts for Hydro-Powered Compute
one_liner: A subscription index that forecasts 30-180 day power-curtailment risk for bitcoin miners and AI data centers on hydro-dependent grids, built from rainfall, inflow and reservoir signals.
customer: Bitcoin mining hosts and data-center operators in hydro-heavy grids (East Africa, southern Africa, Central Asia, Paraguay, Pacific Northwest), plus their lenders, equipment financiers and insurers. Operators and lenders pay.
problem: Step one: Ethiopia cut power to miners by 75% during an El Nino drought, when reservoir inflows fell about 20% in a month. Miners use over a third of a grid that is 90% hydro. Step two: every hydro grid with growing crypto and AI load faces the same triage. Step three: hosts and lenders are financing sites on 'firm cheap green power' contracts with no drought-risk model.
solution: Combine satellite rainfall, soil moisture, snowpack, ENSO outlooks and satellite-measured reservoir levels into a probability of curtailed hours per site. Map it to each grid's known dispatch rules. Backtest against Ethiopia 2026 and the 2024 Kariba (Zambia/Zimbabwe) load-shedding. Deliver a weekly dashboard and a lender-diligence report.
why_now: El Nino drought is live, WMO calls this one of the driest years for the world's rivers in 35 years, and compute loads are chasing cheap hydro. Grids have now made compute-versus-water triage an explicit decision.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per operator portfolio, $10-30k per lender or insurer diligence report, and later an index licensed for parametric cover.
non_obvious_insight: The risk being mispriced is hydrological, not political, and the party who needs the forecast is the compute host's lender, not the grid. A dry year is a correlated credit event across every hydro-powered site.
first_30_days: Build a public-data prototype for five reservoirs. Publish a free weekly brief aimed at miners and hosting firms. Backtest and publish the Ethiopia and Kariba case studies. Pitch three hosting firms and two mining lenders for paid pilots.

title: Bot-Proof Local Comments: Verified Neighbors, Pseudonymous
one_liner: Secret and Yik Yak died of unaccountable anonymity and Digg's March 2026 relaunch died of bots; the missing primitive is 'one real human, from this place, no real name', and local newsrooms and city councils will pay for it.
customer: Independent and nonprofit local newsrooms (hundreds exist) that have switched off comments, and city, county and school-board clerks running public comment for hearings on rezonings, data centers and levies.
problem: Newsrooms disabled comment sections because of toxicity and bots, so local conversation moved to Facebook groups. Public bodies get astroturf and AI-generated comment floods (the 2017 FCC net-neutrality docket was later found mostly fake by New York's attorney general) and cannot tell residents from out-of-area campaigns or bots.
solution: An embeddable comment and public-comment widget. Each person verifies once via a state mobile ID in Apple or Google Wallet with address check, or a postcard PIN or voter-file match as fallback, then posts under a pseudonym. The platform attests only 'verified human, resident of ZIP or ward X'. Public bodies get a verified-resident tally (for example, '412 verified residents commented, 78% opposed, 61 from Ward 3'). One credential works across the paper, council and school board, and publishers never see identity.
why_now: Digg's open beta launched 14 January 2026 and shut on 14 March 2026 after bot and AI-agent floods. Agents can now write plausible public comments at scale. Mobile IDs in phone wallets make cheap, high-assurance verification possible. Local news funders are paying for audience-trust infrastructure.
revenue_model: $200-1,500/mo per newsroom; $500-3,000/mo per municipality or agency for a verified public-comment portal; per-verification fees ($0.50-1.50) sponsored by foundations or civic funders; later, verified local polling panels.
non_obvious_insight: Anonymity was never the fatal flaw; unverifiable anonymity was. In a bot-saturated internet, 'provably a real neighbor' becomes the scarce good, and local institutions already need it but cannot buy it. The credential also compounds: a resident verified once for the newspaper is reusable for council, school board and library levy comments.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 small newsrooms through nonprofit-news networks to run a verified-comment pilot on one hot local issue (rezoning or data center) using SMS or postcard plus voter-file match. Publish the verified-tally story, then pitch the same town's clerk a public-comment pilot. Charge $250/mo after the pilot.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

title: Turf-Ban Pivot Desk for Lawn and Irrigation Crews
angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office x Water (lens: local marketing x utility rebates)
one_liner: A done-for-you back office that turns lawn-maintenance crews into rebate-financed turf-removal and drip-conversion contractors, and uses their weekly routes as a cheap verification network for water utilities.
customer: Independent lawn-care, landscape-maintenance and irrigation companies with 5-40 crew members in drought-restricted Western and Texas metros. Secondary payers are water utilities and conservation funders.
problem: Their core product, mowing and irrigating turf, is being restricted and priced out as drought and utility rules spread. The replacement product (turf removal, drip conversion, native planting) is a project business with estimating, permits, rebate paperwork (pre-inspection photos, invoices, post-inspection) and financing, and national outfits are taking the work. Getting customers is small firms' #1 operational challenge in the Fed's 2026 survey, and legacy local-marketing vendors like Thryv are shrinking.
solution: A rebate-stacking engine per address (utility, county, state, supplier), net-cost-after-rebate estimates, photo-guided pre and post documentation, and submission with follow-up. Bridge financing against assigned rebates. Auto-generated local landing pages, Google Business Profile posts and mailers to the crew's existing maintenance clients ('your street qualifies for $X'). A route-verification add-on where crews photo-confirm turf has stayed removed so utilities can count the savings.
why_now: 49.6% of the US is in drought and the Colorado River 2027-2036 framework forces cuts. $7.2B of FY2026 SRF money is flowing. Corporate water-positive money, such as Amazon's $20M into the Water Resilience Coalition, increasingly needs verified savings that can be counted. Lower-cost LLM tooling makes per-address rebate rules and local pages cheap to produce for a 10-person crew.
revenue_model: 10% of rebate dollars processed (rebates on a job commonly run from several hundred to a few thousand dollars). 2% per month on bridge advances. $199/mo marketing add-on. $25-$60 per site per year from utilities or funders for route verification.
non_obvious_insight: The crew's client list and weekly route are the real assets. They are the only workforce already at every yard every week, which makes them both the best sales channel for turf conversion and a near-zero-cost inspection network to catch re-sodding, the thing utilities and funders need before they trust rebate savings. The subsidy is a sales script, not the product.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a large turf rebate program. Find 5 lawn companies through the local green-industry association. Process 10 of their pending rebates free, then charge 10%. Publish a 'net cost after rebates' page for each crew's service area. Pitch one utility on a paid route-verification pilot covering 200 sites.
